claims.text: The onset and progression of phase transitions in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are governed by an interplay between surface-energy reduction and atomic diffusion.
Surface-to-volume ratio critically determines the temperature range of the phase transitions.
Increasing temperature enhances the mobility of surface atoms because they experience reduced cohesive forces.
Enhanced surface-atom mobility leads to minimization of surface energy.
The higher surface-to-volume ratio of smaller nanoparticles accelerates surface-energy minimization.
Premelting initiates at lower temperatures in smaller FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles than in larger ones.
Atomic diffusion redistributes the constituent elements and thereby further drives the phase transition.
Smaller nanoparticles will have a narrower temperature interval for complete melting than larger nanoparticles.
The phase transition will progress more abruptly in smaller nanoparticles because their surface-energy contribution is higher.
Premelting effects are negligible in larger bulk FeNiCrCoCu samples.
Bulk FeNiCrCoCu samples melt at a well-defined temperature.
An inert atmosphere prevents oxidation during the temperature ramp.
The proposed mechanism applies to FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles with diameters from 5 to 20 nm under inert atmospheric conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to significantly larger particles or particles heated under reactive atmospheres.
